chapter_title: The SOLID Principles - Part 2 (LSP, ISP & DIP)

screens.title: SOLID Principles — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion

narration.text: In this lesson we continue with the SOLID family, focusing on three principles that shape how systems stay flexible as they grow. First, you will learn the Liskov Substitution Principle, which ensures derived types can stand in for their base types without breaking behavior. Then we will examine the Interface Segregation Principle, which prevents clients from depending on large, unfocused interfaces. Finally, we will cover the Dependency Inversion Principle, and see dependency injection in practice so high-level code depends on abstractions instead of concrete details. Throughout the chapter you will examine concrete C# examples: the Bird and Penguin case to reveal an LSP violation, a multi-function device to demonstrate ISP, and logger/order-processor and payment gateway examples to practice DIP and constructor injection. These principles matter because they reduce brittle code, simplify testing, and make feature changes safer. By the end you will be able to spot violations, refactor to focused interfaces and abstractions, and wire dependencies at composition roots. Consider how these patterns change the way you design classes and interfaces in your next real project.

keyIdea.title: Why these principles matter
keyIdea.text: They prevent brittle inheritance, avoid fat interfaces, and decouple modules so systems are testable and maintainable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — part A

narration.text: These objectives map to practical skills you will use in C# projects. First, you will be able to explain the Liskov Substitution Principle: that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without changing program correctness. This matters because improper inheritance breaks client code at runtime, as the Bird and Penguin example shows. Second, you will be able to apply the Interface Segregation Principle to design focused interfaces so classes only implement behaviors they actually need. Smaller interfaces reduce unnecessary NotSupportedExceptions and make implementations simpler. Third, you will understand the Dependency Inversion Principle, recognizing that high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete types, which gives you loose coupling. Fourth, you will demonstrate dependency injection techniques such as constructor injection to satisfy DIP, making components easy to test and swap. Each objective links to a small milestone so you can verify competency by reading a short refactor, implementing an interface split, or writing a constructor-injected test double. These goals are deliberately practical: you will refactor example code, create interfaces, and show how composition roots wire implementations, so you can apply the same patterns in your own codebase.

screens.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
screens.subtitle: What substitutability means and why behavior matters

narration.text: Liskov Substitution Principle is a guarantee about behavior: a subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is expected without changing the correctness of the program. Practically, this means the public contract expressed by a base class or interface sets expectations for clients. If a derived class breaks those expectations — for example by throwing exceptions on calls clients assume are safe — substitution fails and client code can crash. A clear concrete example appears in the Bird/Penguin case: when Bird exposes a Fly method, client code that asks every Bird to fly will fail if a Penguin is present. That tells us the abstraction was wrong. The correct approach is to move flying behavior into an IFlyable interface and make only flying birds implement it. This preserves substitutability for Bird and still allows Penguin to be a Bird without a Fly method. A common misconception is to keep everything in the base class for convenience; this leads to overloaded base types and hidden runtime errors. The takeaway: design base types around behaviors all subtypes can satisfy, and extract separate interfaces for optional capabilities. Ask yourself: if I substitute this subtype, will every promised action still hold?

keyIdea.title: LSP in one line
keyIdea.text: Design abstractions so every concrete subtype honors the base type's behavioral contract.

content.html:
Core Concept
Liskov Substitution Principle
Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering correctness.
Definition & intuition

LSP focuses on behavioral contracts. If clients rely on certain behavior, that behavior must remain true for all derived types. Otherwise substitution breaks.

Common mistake

Putting optional behavior in the base class and using NotSupportedException or empty bodies in derived types hides violations until runtime.

Key Takeaway

Refactor optional behavior into separate interfaces so substitutability remains safe.

Concrete example (Bird / Penguin)
public class Bird
{
  public virtual void Fly()
  {
    Console.WriteLine("Bird is flying.");
  }
}

public class Penguin : Bird
{
  public override void Fly()
  {
    // Violates LSP: penguin cannot fly and throws
    throw new NotSupportedException("Penguins cannot fly!");
  }
}
This design causes client code that expects to call Fly on every Bird to fail. The safe refactor extracts IFlyable and only flying birds implement it.
Analogy
Don't promise features to every subtype; only those that can deliver should be included in the contract.
Common Mistake
Using exceptions or no-ops to satisfy a base class method is a sign the abstraction is wrong.

screens.title: LSP Violation — Bird / Penguin Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Read the failing example and understand why it breaks substitutability

narration.text: Let's walk through the Bird and Penguin example step by step so you can hear why it violates substitutability. The base Bird class defines a Fly method that, by its presence, promises clients they can invoke Fly on any Bird instance. The Penguin class inherits Bird but cannot perform flying; overriding Fly to throw NotSupportedException breaks the promise. If client code iterates a list of Bird and calls Fly on each element, the presence of a Penguin results in a runtime exception and possibly application failure. The core issue is a mismatch between the abstraction and the range of valid implementations. The correct pattern is to keep Bird focused on behaviors common to all birds, like Eat or Species, and extract flying into an IFlyable interface. Then only Sparrow and other flying birds implement IFlyable. A misconception to watch for is thinking inheritance is only about code reuse; it's primarily about substitutability. Reusing code by putting methods in a base type is convenient, but if not all subtypes can honor the behavior, the base type is the wrong place. As you refactor, update client code to depend on IFlyable when flying is required, and keep Bird as the minimal common abstraction.

keyIdea.title: Read code as contract
keyIdea.text: A method on a base type is a promise to clients; only keep promises that every subtype can fulfill.

content.html:
Definition
Violation example
Failing code
public class Bird
{
  public virtual void Fly()
  {
    Console.WriteLine("Bird is flying.");
  }
}

public class Penguin : Bird // Penguin cannot fly
{
  public override void Fly()
  {
    throw new NotSupportedException("Penguins cannot fly!");
  }
}

public class Aviary
{
  public void MakeBirdsFly(List<Bird> birds)
  {
    foreach (var bird in birds)
    {
      bird.Fly(); // Crashes if a Penguin is present
    }
  }
}
Why this breaks substitution
  • Base type promises Fly; clients rely on that promise.
  • Pigeon or Sparrow honor Fly; Penguin cannot, so substitution fails.
  • Runtime exceptions reveal the contract mismatch late.
Safe refactor
public interface IFlyable { void Fly(); }

public class Sparrow : Bird, IFlyable { public void Fly() { /* ... */ } }
public class Penguin : Bird { public void Swim() { /* ... */ } }
After the refactor, Aviary should only call Fly on IFlyable collections, and Bird remains the common, substitutable abstraction for non-flying behaviors.

screens.title: Refactoring to Respect LSP
screens.subtitle: Steps to extract behavior and keep substitution safe

narration.text: Refactoring for LSP is a deliberate, low-risk process. Begin by identifying which methods in a base type are optional for some subtypes. For each optional method, ask whether every subclass can meaningfully implement it. If the answer is no, prepare to extract a focused interface. Next, implement the new interface on only the types that can fulfill that contract. Update client code so it depends on the interface only when it needs that behavior; for example, make a MakeFlyablesFly method accept a collection of IFlyable instead of Bird. Run tests to confirm no behavioral change for unrelated code paths. A helpful tip is to write a small targeted unit test that exercises the refactor: create a Sparrow, ensure Fly is available, create a Penguin, ensure it does not implement IFlyable, and confirm that calling Fly is not attempted on Penguin. A common misconception is that extracting interfaces creates fragmentation; instead, the goal is coherence: group related methods clients actually use together. Finally, avoid premature atomization — group behaviors that naturally belong together so interfaces remain useful and discoverable. The result is an inheritance hierarchy that safely supports substitution and clearer client contracts.

keyIdea.title: Refactor checklist
keyIdea.text: Identify optional behavior, extract focused interfaces, update clients, and run targeted tests.

content.html:
Process Flow
Refactor for LSP
A short, safe sequence to move optional behavior into interfaces.
1. Detect optional methods
Find base methods that not all subclasses can implement.
2. Extract interface
Create a focused interface for the optional behavior, e.g., IFlyable.
3. Implement selectively
Only types that can perform behavior implement the new interface.
4. Update clients
Change client signatures to accept the focused interface when needed.
5. Test
Add unit tests to assert correct substitutability and no regressions.
Example client adjustments
// Before
public void MakeBirdsFly(List<Bird> birds)
{
  foreach (var bird in birds) bird.Fly();
}

// After
public void MakeFlyablesFly(List<IFlyable> flyables)
{
  foreach (var f in flyables) f.Fly();
}
Pro‑Tip
Run small focused tests for each behavior to ensure new interfaces meet expectations.
Pitfall
Avoid creating an interface per method; group closely related operations.

screens.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
screens.subtitle: Why fat interfaces harm implementers and clients

narration.text: The Interface Segregation Principle states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. In practice, this means avoid large, monolithic interfaces that bundle unrelated responsibilities. When a class implements a fat interface, it may be forced to provide method bodies it doesn't need, leading to NotSupportedException or empty implementations. The multi-function device example demonstrates this: a BasicPrinter forced to implement scanning, faxing, copying, and stapling—capabilities it doesn't have—becomes brittle and confusing. ISP tells us to design smaller, role-specific interfaces such as IPrinter, IScanner, and IStapler. This makes classes simpler and clients more focused because they depend only on the operations they require. A common misconception is that many tiny interfaces increase complexity; the right balance groups related methods that clients commonly use together. The practical advantage is clearer contracts and reduced coupling, and it often prevents LSP-style problems where a class pretends to support behavior it cannot actually perform. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) means prefer many small interfaces grouped by client needs rather than one large interface.. In practical terms, why fat interfaces harm implementers and clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ISP in one line
keyIdea.text: Prefer many small interfaces grouped by client needs rather than one large interface.

content.html:
Core Concept
Interface Segregation Principle
Clients should not depend on methods they don't use.
Fat interface problem
public interface IMultiFunctionDevice
{
  void Print(string document);
  void Scan(string document);
  void Fax(string document);
  void Copy(string document);
  void Staple(string document);
}
When a BasicPrinter implements this interface it is forced into NotSupportedException stubs for many methods it doesn't support. That is brittle and violates ISP.
Segregated interfaces
public interface IPrinter { void Print(string document); }
public interface IScanner { void Scan(string document); }
public interface IFaxMachine { void Fax(string document); }
public interface IStapler { void Staple(string document); }
Now BasicPrinter implements only IPrinter, and OfficeMultiFunctionDevice can implement the set it actually supports. This reduces coupling and accidental runtime errors.
Analogy
Give clients the exact toolset they need, not a tool chest they will ignore.
Warning
Don't over-segregate: group methods that clients naturally use together.

screens.title: ISP Violation — MultiFunction Device Example
screens.subtitle: See how a fat interface forces unsupported implementations

narration.text: Examine the IMultiFunctionDevice example to see how ISP violations manifest. The interface lists Print, Scan, Fax, Copy, and Staple. A BasicPrinter that only prints is forced to implement scanning and faxing with NotSupportedException, which is a code smell. This not only increases code complexity but also moves errors to runtime when a client mistakenly calls a method the implementation doesn't actually support. The refactor is straightforward: split responsibilities into IPrinter, IScanner, IFaxMachine, and IStapler. Then BasicPrinter implements only IPrinter while an OfficeMultiFunctionDevice implements the full set it supports. This reduces coupling and clarifies client dependencies. A common misconception is to keep a single interface for convenience or perceived discoverability; instead, design interfaces around client needs. When refactoring, consider grouping methods into interfaces that reflect a coherent role, and avoid creating an interface per method unless that method is truly independent. The net effect of ISP is more predictable implementations and fewer runtime surprises, and it helps tests focus on the behavior that matters to each client. ISP Violation — MultiFunction Device Example means if a class throws notsupportedexception for interface methods, the interface should be split.. In practical terms, see how a fat interface forces unsupported implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ISP practical rule
keyIdea.text: If a class throws NotSupportedException for interface methods, the interface should be split.

content.html:
Comparison
Fat interface vs Segregated interfaces
Fat interface
public interface IMultiFunctionDevice
{
  void Print(string document);
  void Scan(string document);
  void Fax(string document);
  void Copy(string document);
  void Staple(string document);
}
BasicPrinter must implement methods it doesn't support, which leads to NotSupportedException and brittle code.
Segregated interfaces
public interface IPrinter { void Print(string document); }
public interface IScanner { void Scan(string document); }
public interface IFaxMachine { void Fax(string document); }
public interface IStapler { void Staple(string document); }
After segregation, each device implements only the interfaces it actually supports, making client dependencies explicit and safe.
Pro‑Tip

Group behaviors by role, not by implementation convenience. This creates interfaces that reflect real client usage.

screens.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
screens.subtitle: Invert dependencies so high-level modules rely on abstractions

narration.text: The Dependency Inversion Principle flips the typical dependency direction: high-level business modules should not depend directly on low-level concrete implementations. Instead, both should depend on abstractions, and details should depend on those abstractions. This principle reduces coupling and makes code easier to test and change. For example, if an OrderProcessor directly constructs a SqlDatabaseLogger, swapping to a FileLogger or a mock for testing requires modifying the OrderProcessor. By introducing an ILogger abstraction and making OrderProcessor depend on ILogger, different concrete loggers can be provided at composition time without changing the business logic. Dependency injection is the practical pattern used to supply concrete implementations for those abstractions, commonly via constructor injection in C#. A common mistake is to new up dependencies inside high-level classes, which tightly couples them. The real benefit of DIP is testability and maintainability: you can inject a mock logger during unit tests and a production logger at startup. Consider wiring dependencies at a single composition root to keep object creation centralized and transparent. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) means depend on interfaces or abstractions, not concrete classes, to enable flexible substitution.. In practical terms, invert dependencies so high-level modules rely on abstractions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DIP in one line
keyIdea.text: Depend on interfaces or abstractions, not concrete classes, to enable flexible substitution.

content.html:
Core Concept
Dependency Inversion Principle
Invert dependencies so modules depend on stable abstractions.
Rule summary
  • High-level modules should depend on abstractions.
  • Abstractions should not depend on details.
  • Details should implement abstractions.
DIP motivation

When you remove direct construction from high-level code, you can substitute implementations for testing or to change technologies without touching business logic. Composition roots centralize creation so the rest of the code remains unaware of concrete classes.

Key Takeaway

Use interfaces for dependencies and inject them at the application's composition root to keep business logic stable.

screens.title: DIP Violation — Logger and OrderProcessor
screens.subtitle: See why new-ing dependencies in high-level modules is fragile

narration.text: Here is a classic DIP violation: a high-level OrderProcessor creates a SqlDatabaseLogger internally. That direct instantiation couples the business logic to a concrete database logger. The problems are immediate: to change the logging mechanism you must modify OrderProcessor, and unit-testing OrderProcessor becomes harder because it uses a real logger that may touch the database. The fix is to introduce an ILogger interface and have OrderProcessor accept an ILogger through constructor injection. Concrete implementations such as SqlDatabaseLogger or FileLogger then implement ILogger. At application startup, the composition root decides which implementation to provide. For tests you can inject a mock ILogger. A common misconception is that passing interfaces around adds ceremony; in reality it separates concerns cleanly — creation is a different responsibility from using a dependency. When refactoring, first extract the interface, update the high-level constructor to accept it, and move the new expression to the composition root. This establishes the pattern for swapping implementations without touching business logic. DIP Violation — Logger and OrderProcessor means move dependency creation out of the business class, depend on ilogger, and inject implementations at startup.. In practical terms, see why new-ing dependencies in high-level modules is fragile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: From new to inject
keyIdea.text: Move dependency creation out of the business class, depend on ILogger, and inject implementations at startup.

content.html:
Violation code
public class SqlDatabaseLogger
{
  public void LogError(string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"SQL DB Logger: Logging error '{message}' to database.");
  }
}

public class OrderProcessor
{
  private SqlDatabaseLogger _logger;

  public OrderProcessor()
  {
    _logger = new SqlDatabaseLogger(); // Direct instantiation
  }

  public void ProcessOrder(int orderId)
  {
    try { /* process */ }
    catch (Exception ex) { _logger.LogError(ex.Message); }
  }
}
Refactor outline
public interface ILogger { void LogError(string message); }
public class SqlDatabaseLogger : ILogger { /* ... */ }
public class OrderProcessor
{
  private readonly ILogger _logger;
  public OrderProcessor(ILogger logger) { _logger = logger; }
}

// At composition root:
ILogger logger = new SqlDatabaseLogger();
var processor = new OrderProcessor(logger);
This refactor enables unit tests to inject a mock ILogger and production code to choose a real implementation at startup. It isolates responsibility for object creation to the composition root.

screens.title: Dependency Injection Patterns
screens.subtitle: Constructor, property and method injection with testability in mind

narration.text: Dependency injection is the technique used to satisfy DIP in practice. The most common pattern is constructor injection: the high-level module receives its dependencies through its constructor and stores them in readonly fields. This pattern makes dependencies explicit, helps with immutability, and is ideal for unit testing. Property injection sets dependencies via public setters and is less explicit — useful for optional dependencies but riskier for required ones. Method injection passes a dependency into individual methods and can be appropriate when a dependency is only needed for a single operation. The chapter examples emphasize constructor injection because it clearly expresses required collaborators and works well with DI frameworks. For testing, constructor injection makes it trivial to supply a mock implementation. A common mistake is to mix direct construction and injection, which undermines the benefits. The composition root is the dedicated place where concrete wiring happens, usually at application startup; keep it small and well-documented. When choosing an injection style, prefer constructor injection for required services and property or method injection for optional or contextual dependencies. Dependency Injection Patterns means prefer constructor injection for required dependencies and wire implementations in the composition root for testability.. In practical terms, constructor, property and method injection with testability in mind. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Injection guidance
keyIdea.text: Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies and wire implementations in the composition root for testability.

content.html:
Architecture
Constructor Injection
public class OrderProcessor
{
  private readonly ILogger _logger;
  public OrderProcessor(ILogger logger)
  {
    _logger = logger; // Injected dependency
  }
}
This approach makes OrderProcessor easy to test because you can pass a mock ILogger from your unit test harness.
Property Injection
Useful for optional dependencies but less explicit. Example: public ILogger Logger { get; set; }
Method Injection
Pass dependency only to the method that needs it: void Process(ILogger logger) — good for transient collaborators.
Composition Root
Centralize object creation at startup. This is where you decide which concrete implementations satisfy abstractions for the whole application.

screens.title: Hands-on: PaymentGateway DIP Refactor
screens.subtitle: Refactor a direct-instantiation gateway into an injected design

narration.text: In this hands-on scenario you will refactor a PaymentGateway that directly creates a CreditCardProcessor, which violates DIP. The task is to introduce an IPaymentProcessor abstraction, make CreditCardProcessor implement it, add a PayPalProcessor implementation, and change PaymentGateway to accept an IPaymentProcessor via constructor injection. Then show how Program. cs wires the concrete processor at startup and demonstrates processing both payment types. The important steps: identify the direct instantiation, extract the IPaymentProcessor interface with a Process method, implement the interface on both processors, update PaymentGateway to depend on the abstraction, and move new to Program. cs where you create a gateway with the desired processor. This approach decouples PaymentGateway from concrete payment processors, enabling tests to inject a fake processor that records calls instead of making financial transactions. A common pitfall is forgetting to update all call sites; ensure you change object construction everywhere and keep a single composition root. After the refactor, switching payment providers requires only a change in the composition root, not in the PaymentGateway itself. Hands-on: PaymentGateway DIP Refactor means introduce ipaymentprocessor and inject it into paymentgateway; wire concrete processors at startup.. In practical terms, refactor a direct-instantiation gateway into an injected design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PaymentGateway refactor
keyIdea.text: Introduce IPaymentProcessor and inject it into PaymentGateway; wire concrete processors at startup.

content.html:
Starter code (violates DIP)
// PaymentGateway constructs CreditCardProcessor directly
public class PaymentGateway
{
  private CreditCardProcessor _creditCardProcessor;

  public PaymentGateway()
  {
    _creditCardProcessor = new CreditCardProcessor(); // Direct instantiation
  }

  public void InitiatePayment(PaymentRequest request)
  {
    if (request.PaymentMethod == "CreditCard")
    {
      _creditCardProcessor.Process(request);
    }
    else
    {
      Console.WriteLine($"Payment method '{request.PaymentMethod}' not supported by this gateway version.");
    }
  }
}
Refactor steps
  1. Extract IPaymentProcessor with Process method.
  2. Make CreditCardProcessor implement IPaymentProcessor.
  3. Create PayPalProcessor implementing IPaymentProcessor.
  4. Change PaymentGateway to accept IPaymentProcessor in constructor.
  5. Wire concrete implementations in Program.cs.
Why this helps
PaymentGateway no longer knows about payment types. Tests can inject a mock processor to simulate transactions without external calls.

screens.title: Combining Principles — When ISP, LSP and DIP Interact
screens.subtitle: How interface design, inheritance, and dependency wiring work together

narration.text: These three SOLID principles are complementary. A fat interface that breaks ISP can lead to LSP-style violations, because classes may implement methods they cannot realistically support. For example, forcing a Penguin to implement Fly via a fat Bird interface results in thrown exceptions and broken substitution. Separating behavior via ISP prevents that. Similarly, when high-level modules depend directly on concrete classes, they may also be forced to implement or mock behaviors that belong to lower-level concerns; applying DIP and injecting abstractions removes that burden. In practice, follow a simple sequence when designing: define small, role-focused interfaces (ISP), ensure base classes only expose behaviors shared by all subtypes (LSP), and make consumers depend on those abstractions, wiring concrete implementations at the composition root (DIP). A common misconception is to treat these principles independently; instead, use them together to make systems cohesive and easy to test. The end result is code where substitutability holds, interfaces reflect real client needs, and high-level logic stays isolated from implementation detail. Combining Principles — When ISP, LSP and DIP Interact means isp, lsp, and dip reinforce one another: focused interfaces, correct abstractions, and injected dependencies create robust designs.. In practical terms, how interface design, inheritance, and dependency wiring work together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Principles together
keyIdea.text: ISP, LSP, and DIP reinforce one another: focused interfaces, correct abstractions, and injected dependencies create robust designs.

content.html:
Best Practice
How the principles fit together
Use ISP to create role-specific interfaces, LSP to keep base types minimal and substitutable, and DIP to decouple high-level modules by depending on those interfaces. This reduces runtime surprises and makes testing and changing implementations straightforward.
ISP → smaller, clearer interfaces
Prevents unnecessary method implementations.
LSP → safe inheritance
Ensure substitutability by keeping base types honest.
DIP → inject abstractions
High-level logic depends on interfaces, not concrete classes.
Scenario comparison
If you see NotSupportedExceptions, large interfaces, and many new expressions in business classes, you likely have combined ISP, LSP, and DIP violations. Fixing one often helps the others: splitting interfaces reduces false inheritance, and injecting abstractions removes the need to fake implementations.
Check your understanding
Can you point to a class in your codebase that constructs its own dependencies and also implements methods that throw NotSupportedException? That class is a candidate for these refactors.

narration.text: Let's capture the essential takeaways. First, LSP requires that derived types behave in ways the base type promises; if some subclasses cannot honor a method, extract that behavior into a separate interface. Second, ISP encourages many focused interfaces so clients depend only on what they use; avoid forcing classes to implement unrelated methods. Third, DIP asks that high-level modules depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations, enabling easy swapping and testing. Also remember dependency injection as the practical technique to supply implementations at a composition root, and that constructor injection is usually the cleanest form for required services. These ideas work together: small interfaces prevent substitutability problems, and abstractions let high-level code remain stable while implementations evolve. Keep these principles in mind when you design or refactor: they help you create maintainable, testable C# applications.

keyIdea.title: Three quick rules
keyIdea.text: Extract optional behavior, split fat interfaces, and inject abstractions at startup.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Key Concepts
Liskov Substitution
Subtypes must honor the base type's behavioral contract so clients can substitute safely.
Interface Segregation
Prefer small interfaces grouped by client needs to avoid NotSupportedExceptions.
Dependency Inversion
High-level modules depend on abstractions. Wire concrete implementations at the composition root.
Summary Takeaway

Design small interfaces, keep base classes honest, and inject dependencies to make systems maintainable and testable.

narration.text: Before you leave, memorize three pragmatic reminders. One: if a class throws NotSupportedException for interface methods, split the interface — that is an ISP smell. Two: if a subtype cannot perform a base class operation, extract that operation to a separate interface so LSP holds. Three: if your high-level class new-s up low-level details, move creation to the composition root and inject an abstraction instead to satisfy DIP. These are quick heuristics you can use during code review and refactoring. In practice, use constructor injection for required services and keep wiring centralized so your code remains easy to change and test. As a final question to guide your next refactor: can I replace this concrete dependency with a simple interface and a test double without changing the high-level module? If yes, apply DIP.

keyIdea.title: Quick heuristics
keyIdea.text: NotSupportedException → ISP; optional base behavior → LSP; new in business logic → DIP and inject.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Reminders
ISP heuristic
If implementers throw NotSupportedException, split the interface.
LSP heuristic
If any subtype can't honor a method, that method shouldn't be on the base type.
DIP heuristic
If a class constructs a dependency, consider extracting an interface and injecting it.
Final Prompt

Before refactoring, ask: can this dependency be replaced by an abstraction and a test double without changing the high-level logic?
